question: Which statement best describes WCAG & the POUR principles?
options: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines organize accessibility into four principles — Perceivable (content can be sensed, e.g. alt text, captions), Operable (everything works by keyboard), Understandable (clear, predictable UI and language), and Robust (works across browsers and assistive tech). Conformance levels are A, AA (the common legal target), and AAA.

Every interactive element must be reachable and usable with the keyboard alone (Tab to move, Enter/Space to activate). Keep a visible focus indicator (never remove outline without a replacement), maintain a logical tab order (follow DOM order; avoid positive tabindex), and manage focus in modals and dynamic content.

Every needs an alt attribute. Describe the image's purpose concisely for content images; use an empty alt="" for purely decorative images so screen readers skip them. Don't start with 'image of' (the reader already says that), and convey the information the image carries, not its filename.

The first rule of accessibility is to use the right native element. A <button> is focusable, keyboard-operable, and announced as a button for free; a <div onclick> is none of those without extra work. Native semantics populate the accessibility tree correctly, so reach for ARIA only when no element fits.

Browsers build an accessibility tree from the DOM — a model of each element's role, name, state, and value. Screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS) read this tree aloud and let users navigate by landmarks and headings. Semantic HTML and correct labels populate it accurately; div soup leaves it empty and confusing.
